concept.name: Confidence calibration
concept.definition: The property that a model's stated confidence matches its true correctness likelihood: among predictions made with 80% confidence, about 80% should be correct. Guo et al. (2017) showed modern deep networks are typically poorly calibrated (overconfident) and that simple post-processing such as temperature scaling can substantially fix it.
concept.intuition: A well-calibrated model's 'I'm 90% sure' is right nine times out of ten — its confidence number means what it says.
concept.mechanics: Calibration is measured with reliability diagrams and metrics such as Expected Calibration Error (bin predictions by confidence, compare average confidence to empirical accuracy). Miscalibration is corrected post-hoc by rescaling the output distribution, e.g., dividing logits by a learned temperature before the softmax.
concept.formula: ECE = Σ_m (|B_m|/n) · |acc(B_m) − conf(B_m)|, where predictions are binned into M bins B_m by confidence, acc(B_m) is empirical accuracy in bin m, conf(B_m) is average predicted confidence in bin m, and n is the total number of predictions.
concept.failure_modes: Calibration is distribution-dependent: it breaks under data or concept drift, so a model calibrated at validation time becomes overconfident in production. Raw LLM verbalized confidence ('I'm fairly sure') is generally much worse calibrated than classifier probabilities.
concept.misconceptions: High accuracy does not imply good calibration — a model can be accurate and systematically overconfident. Softmax probabilities are not calibrated confidences by default; calibration must be measured and usually corrected.
concept.example: A signal classifier says 0.9 confidence on 100 trades; if only 70 are correct, it is overconfident — after temperature scaling, its 0.9-confidence bucket actually wins about 90% of the time.

citations.source: Guo et al., 'On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks' (ICML 2017)
